content.thinking:
I need to avoid citing any numbers myself and instead reference figures by their labels. I'm outlining the causal chain starting from the symptom of stale spend totals on account pages, noting that a portion of cached figures disagreed with actual purchases, and tracing this back to the caching mechanism as the likely root cause.

The entries fell behind the ledger because whatever fills the cache stopped keeping pace around a certain point, while the read path served any cached entry without verifying it against the ledger. Nothing refreshes or evicts stale entries when a shopper buys again, and since deploys and flags show zero changes and logs/metrics are empty during the relevant window, the actual trigger for why the cache fill stalled remains unclear -- so while I can identify the stale caching mechanism as the proximate cause, the root trigger itself isn't shown in the evidence.

I'm identifying the contributing factors: no validation check on the read path, detection only occurring after a long divergence window with no freshness alerting, and the fact that discarding stale entries is just a one-off fix rather than a durable solution. I'm planning new numbered action items beyond the existing AI-1 and AI-2 — one to investigate why the cache fill stopped, and another to add alerting on cache feed lag.

I'm drafting three new action items: finding why the cache-filling process stopped keeping up and fixing it (plus adding purchase-triggered invalidation), alerting on cache fill lag before reconciliation, and restoring metrics/logs capture since they returned nothing during the incident. I'm noting I shouldn't propose confirming root cause as a separate item, and starting to sketch the lessons-learned section — what went well (quick mitigation, draft fix PR), what went wrong (unreadable telemetry, only a temporary discard fix), and what got lucky (no errors or latency impact).

Now I'm working through the "lucky" angle more carefully: the ledger never moved during the incident so the fallback behaved correctly, meaning staleness was bounded to at most one purchase — that's the real lucky break, not just flat metrics. I'm also listing assumptions to flag: incident duration is a lower bound, error rate is unknown, the root cause of the feed stopping wasn't identified, and the alert's trigger time reflects when the check ran rather than when staleness actually began. I'm double-checking I'm not accidentally putting stray digits into prose where only clean names should appear.

action_items.item: Find out why the process that fills the cached spend totals stopped keeping up at about {A5}. Repair it, and make a purchase refresh or evict the shopper's entry so the copies do not depend on the feed alone.
Add an alert on how far the cache feed lags behind the purchase ledger, so a stall is flagged before the reconciliation check finds many wrong figures.
Find out why the metrics and log reads for io-shop returned nothing during this incident, and restore them so the next investigation can see error rate, latency and feed activity.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw spend totals on their account pages that were behind their real purchases. {A1} of {A2} cached figures disagreed with the purchase ledger. The widest gap was {A3}, and no figure was missing more than {A4} purchase. No errors or latency change were reported.

The cached copies were behind the ledger, and the ledger itself was correct. The copies stopped keeping up at {A5}, the time of the oldest purchase they did not account for. Discarding the stale entries sent those pages back to the ledger and the store reported removing {T20.2} entries, which supports the finding that only the cache copies were wrong.

The page showed the stale figures because it served any entry the cache returned, as is, without checking it against the account's purchases. This is from a static reading of `account_page._the_figure_for` that nothing ran, so it is unverified.

Stale entries stayed stale because, by the same unverified reading, nothing in the service refreshes or evicts an entry when its shopper buys again. Once whatever fills the cache fell behind, nothing else corrected the copies. The alert says the same: nothing is putting the copies right, so a figure goes stale as soon as its shopper buys again.

The record does not show why the cache feed stopped keeping up. No production changes were read back and the flag provider showed no recent flag changes, so a deploy or flag change is ruled out as the trigger. The metrics and log reads returned nothing, so the record holds no evidence about the feed itself. The chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The read path serves cached entries without validating them against the account's purchases, and no purchase-time refresh or eviction was seen. Any lapse in the cache feed therefore reaches shoppers directly. The proposed fix is still open.
The cause of the cache feed falling behind is not known, and the discard mitigation is not a lasting repair. Nothing was seen that keeps the copies correct, so entries go stale again as shoppers buy.
Detection came only from the reconciliation check, which fired for a divergence that had already begun at {A5}. No earlier alert on the cache feed lagging was seen.

The investigation could not see the service. The metrics read returned {T5.2} minutes and the log read returned {T11.2} lines, so the error rate is unknown and the start of the fault and the state of the feed could not be checked.

input.executive_summary: Some shoppers' account pages showed a spend total that was behind their real purchases. The purchase records were correct throughout. Only the stored copies of the totals were out of date. The check found {A1} of {A2} stored totals wrong, with the widest gap at {A3}. The copies had stopped keeping up at {A5}. The incident was open for at least {duration}, which is a lower bound. Argus discarded the stale stored totals, so those pages went back to the purchase records. It then proposed a code fix as a draft pull request that is still open. Nothing was seen that keeps the stored totals correct, so they can go stale again until that fix or a feed repair lands. The reason the copies stopped keeping up was not found.

got_lucky: The purchase ledger never moved, so falling back to it gave correct figures.
No errors or latency change were reported, and no figure was missing more than {A4} purchase, so the visible harm was limited to out-of-date totals.
went_well: Argus discarded the stale entries and the store reported what it removed, so the mitigation was confirmed. The affected pages went back to the correct ledger.
A draft pull request was proposed that makes the page check each entry's purchase count, so it no longer depends on the cache feed being healthy.
went_wrong: The metrics and log reads came back empty, so the investigation rested on the alert text and a static code reading.
The discard clears only the entries that were wrong at that moment. Nothing was seen that keeps the copies correct, so later purchases can make them stale again.
The reason the feed stopped keeping up is still unknown.

input.root_cause: The cached per-shopper spend totals stopped keeping up with the purchase ledger, and nothing in io-shop corrected them. By the code reading, which was not run, nothing refreshes or evicts an entry when its shopper buys again, and the account page serves whatever entry the cache returns without checking it. Once the cache feed fell behind, every later purchase left an older figure on the page. The record does not show why the feed stopped keeping up.
input.symptom: Account pages showed out-of-date spend totals
